newsitem.title: GERMANY: MG raises funds to expand with bank sale.
newsitem.headline: MG raises funds to expand with bank sale.

text.p: Metallgesellschaft AG, the German industrial and trading group which ran into huge losses in 1993, said on Wednesday it was selling its banking unit and that the funds raised could be used to make an acquisition.

MG, which is only now finding its feet again after booking billions of marks of losses on risky U.S. oil deals in its 1993/94 business year, said it was selling the its Metallbank subsidiary to Bavarian private bank Schmidtbank KGaA.

No financial details were disclosed, but MG spokesman Andreas Martin said the company had gained a "good price". The book profit from the sale would flow into the company's 1996/97 balance sheet, he added.
MG made clear the funds raised could be used for expansion, saying. "MG is improving its balance sheet total considerably and is gaining room to manoeuvre on acquisitions."
The announcement of the Metallbank sale was just the most recent in a long line of divestments at MG as part of an extensive restructuring programme.

The new slimmed-down MG, which reported a pretax profit of 171 million marks in its 1994/95 business year -- a sharp turnaround from the 1993/94 loss of over 2.54 billion marks -- will report its profits for the year to September 30 on Friday.

Analysts generally expect the company to have reached its stated target of profit of at least 300 million marks in 1995/96. Juergen Trojan of Independent Research in Frankfurt, said he expected group pretax profit of 307 million marks.
Trojan added that the funds raised could be used to make an acquisition in plant construction. MG had no comment on this.
In its statement announcing the move, MG said the sale was an early response to consolidation trends in the banking industry and would also help strengthen its balance sheet.
"With this sale, Metallgesellschaft is responding early to the strong process of concentration in the banking sector and is creating new growth and profit opportunities for itself."
MG management board chairman Kajo Neukirchen said the sale increased shareholder value. "The separation from Metallbank has helped us to optimise the group for shareholders," he said.
MG shares, which were suspended briefly immediately after the announcement, resumed trade 42 pfennigs higher at 28 marks, holding that level in late trade.

Asked to elaborate on the strategy behind the sale, Martin said one additional reason lay in changes to laws governing German credit institutions which would prevent Metallbank offering such a high volume of credit to MG's workforce.

The bank, which has a balance sheet total of 1.25 billion marks, employs 147 people and its main activity is in providing bank services for MG itself and its employees. It will retain its name and the same business fields under its new owner.

Martin said MG was also keen to avoid bearing the high investment needed due to the planned introduction of the single European currency. "The conversion will be expensive and commissions will shrink," he said.

The new owner, SchmidtBank, is a private banking group with 130 branches in Bavaria, Saxony and Thuringia. MG said the deal, which is back-dated to October 1, 1996, offered SchmidtBank access to the Frankfurt market.

The Bavarian-based bank had a balance sheet total of 9.9 billion marks in the year to September 1996 and employed 1,812 workers on that day. The bank, founded in 1818, is run by three managing directors, including Karl Gerhard Schmidt.

Neukirchen said the choice of buyer had played an important role in the sale. "The bank had been in the company for 90 years, so it was important for us that it be transferred to the hands of a respected banker," he said.
